passages.happening:
The chapter begins by naming a relative of Naomi's dead husband: ‘a prominent man of noble character from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz’ (verse 1).

Ruth asks Naomi to let her go into the fields and glean grain behind someone who will be kind to her. “Go ahead, my daughter,” Naomi replied (verse 2). Ruth goes, and she gleans behind the harvesters. ‘And she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz’ (verse 3).

Just then Boaz arrives from Bethlehem and greets the harvesters: “The LORD be with you.” They reply, “The LORD bless you” (verse 4). He asks his foreman whose young woman this is. The foreman tells him she is the Moabitess who came back with Naomi, that she asked to glean among the sheaves, and that she has worked from morning until now with hardly a rest (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
The narrator tells the reader about Boaz before Ruth meets him. The Hebrew phrase for him can describe a mighty warrior, but here it means a man of wealth, influence and worth.

Gleaning was a right Israel's law gave to the poor. Landowners were told not to reap to the very edges of their fields or to go back for what fell, and to leave forgotten sheaves for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. Ruth was a foreigner and a widow. But not every landowner kept these laws, and a foreign woman gleaning alone could be mistreated.

‘She happened to come’ is, in Hebrew, something like her chance chanced upon it. The narrator speaks of chance with a wink. The reader is meant to see what Ruth cannot: in this book nothing is really an accident. God's hand is at work through an ordinary choice of where to glean.

The harvest was shared work. Men cut the standing grain with sickles, women bound it into sheaves, and gleaners came behind. Boaz greets his workers in the LORD's name, and they answer in kind. Faith shapes the everyday speech of his household.
passages.later: The law Ruth relies on is in Leviticus: “When you reap the harvest of your land, you are not to reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest” (Leviticus 19:9). And in Deuteronomy: “If you are harvesting in your field and forget a sheaf there, do not go back to get it. It is to be left for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow” (Deuteronomy 24:19).
passages.asks: Ruth went out to work, and the narrator says she ‘happened’ to come to the right field. Ask where in your ordinary week you might be closer to God's hand than you think. And look at Boaz's greeting. Ask whether faith shapes the way you speak to the people who work beside you or for you.

passages.happening:
Boaz speaks to Ruth. She is to stay in his field, close to his servant girls. He has told the young men not to touch her. When she is thirsty she may drink from the jars the young men have filled (verses 8-9).

She bows to the ground. “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?” (verse 10).

Boaz answers that he has heard everything she has done for her mother-in-law since her husband died, how she left her father and mother and her own land to come to a people she did not know (verse 11). “May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge” (verse 12).

At mealtime he invites her to eat with his workers and hands her roasted grain, and she eats until she is satisfied and has some left over (verse 14). When she goes back to glean, he tells his young men to let her gather even among the sheaves, and to pull out stalks from the bundles and leave them for her (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
Boaz does far more than the law required. The law let the poor gather what was left. Boaz gives Ruth protection, water, a place at his table and extra grain left on purpose where she will find it.

His order that the young men not touch her matters. A foreign woman working alone in someone else's field was in danger. Boaz puts her under his protection.

Ruth's question is the question of the whole book: why should a foreigner find favor? Boaz's answer is that he has heard of her loyalty to Naomi. She left her own family and land, as Abraham once did, to come to a people she did not know.

His prayer uses a picture of a bird sheltering its young under its wings. Ruth has come to shelter under the wings of Israel's God. The same Hebrew word, a wing or the corner of a garment, will come back in chapter 3, when Ruth asks Boaz himself to spread the corner of his garment over her. She will be asking him to become the answer to his own prayer.
passages.later:
The psalms use the same picture of God's protection: “He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4).

Abraham, too, left his land and his father's house at God's call: “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you” (Genesis 12:1).
passages.asks: Boaz did more than the law asked, for a foreign woman no one else noticed. Ask whom in your field of work or life you could protect, feed or quietly make room for. And hear Ruth's question, ‘Why have I found such favor?’ Ask whether you have ever been surprised by kindness, and what it taught you about God.

passages.happening:
Ruth gleans until evening and beats out what she has gathered: about an ephah of barley (verse 17). She carries it home, and gives Naomi the food she saved from her meal (verse 18).

Naomi asks where she worked. “Blessed be the man who noticed you.” Ruth tells her that the man's name is Boaz (verse 19).

“May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His kindness from the living or the dead.” Naomi continued, “The man is a close relative. He is one of our kinsman-redeemers” (verse 20).

Ruth tells her that Boaz has said she should stay with his workers until the harvest is done. Naomi agrees: it is good for her to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to her in another field (verses 21-22). So Ruth gleans in Boaz's fields until the barley and wheat harvests are finished, and she lives with her mother-in-law (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
An ephah was a large amount for one day's gleaning. Estimates of its size vary, but it was enough to feed two women for some weeks.

When Naomi hears the name Boaz, everything changes. The woman who came home saying the LORD had brought her back empty now speaks of the LORD's kindness, the same word, chesed, she used on the road in chapter 1. The Hebrew of verse 20 could mean that Boaz's kindness or the LORD's kindness has not stopped. Readers differ, but the point is the same either way: God's faithfulness is reaching Naomi through Boaz's generosity.

A kinsman-redeemer, in Hebrew go'el, was a close relative with the right and the duty to help a family in trouble: to buy back land sold out of the family, to free a relative sold into slavery, or to take up a family's cause. Naomi sees a door opening.

The barley harvest came in spring and the wheat harvest followed, a season of perhaps seven weeks. It is the season between Passover and the Feast of Weeks, which is why Jewish tradition reads Ruth at that feast.
passages.later: The law describes the redeemer's duty: “If your brother becomes impoverished and sells some of his property, his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold” (Leviticus 25:25). The same word is used of God himself: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with mighty acts of judgment” (Exodus 6:6).
passages.asks: Naomi's bitterness began to lift when she saw God's kindness in another person's kindness. Ask whose kindness has been God's kindness to you, and whether you have thanked either of them. And ask whether there is someone whose emptiness you could begin to fill, the way Ruth's barley began to fill Naomi's.
